opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was a panel where several people were asked, roughly, "When do you expect AGI?" and then separately, "What do you think AI will do to jobs?" What struck me was that a lot of the panelists gave fairly aggressive timelines for AGI, like within five or ten years, and then turned around and said something like, "But I'm optimistic about jobs. Historically technology creates more jobs than it destroys, and people will find new kinds of work."

And I just found those two answers really hard to hold in my head at the same time. If you mean AGI in any strong sense, a system that can do basically everything a human worker can do, including learning new tasks, then the historical argument about job creation doesn't obviously carry over. Past technologies automated *particular* tasks, and humans moved into the tasks machines couldn't do. That pattern depends on there being a frontier of things humans are still comparatively better at. If you've built something that can also do whatever the new jobs turn out to be, often more cheaply and faster, then "new jobs will be created" doesn't tell you much, because the AI can take those new jobs too.

So I kept wanting to ask, okay, which is it? Either you don't really mean AGI, and you're picturing something more like a very powerful tool that complements human workers, which is a coherent view and could be right. Or you do mean AGI, and then you need a much more specific story about why humans stay employed. Maybe people value human-made things for their own sake, or there are legal or social reasons certain roles stay human, or comparative advantage keeps some wages positive. But those are pretty different stories, and they don't look much like "the economy has always adapted before."

To me it suggested that people weren't really letting the AGI prediction sink in. They'd say the word and then reason about the labor market as if it were a normal technology. That kind of inconsistency is something I see a lot, and I think it's one of the more important things to push on. If we're actually headed toward systems that can do most cognitive work, the implications for the economy and for society are much bigger and weirder than the standard reassurances allow for.

r001.rationale: The response juxtaposes a five- or ten-year AGI timeline, defined as systems able to do nearly everything a human worker can do, with optimism that jobs will be created, and asks how those predictions fit together.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so what struck me was this tension that nobody on the panel seemed to notice they were holding. On the one hand, several of them said they expected AGI, or something close to it, within the next few years. And then in the same breath, when asked about the labor market, they said the main story would be job creation, that AI would create more jobs than it displaced, the way previous technologies did.

And I just kept thinking, those two things can't both be true in the way they're describing. If you actually mean AGI, if you mean systems that can do essentially any cognitive task a human can do, at human level or better, and cheaper, then the historical analogy to the tractor or the spreadsheet breaks down. The reason past automation created new jobs is that there were always things humans could still do that the machines couldn't. The displaced farmhands moved into factories, the displaced factory workers moved into services. There was always a frontier the technology hadn't reached.

But the whole definition of AGI is that there's no frontier left. Whatever new job you invent, the AI can do that too. So either you don't really believe in AGI on the timeline you just stated, and you're picturing something more like a very good productivity tool, which is fine, but then say that. Or you do believe it, and then the job creation story needs a lot more argument than "this is what's always happened before."

I think what was actually going on is that people were drawing on two different mental models depending on which question they were asked. When you ask about capabilities, they reach for the sci-fi picture. When you ask about economics, they reach for the historical picture. And those pictures haven't been reconciled. That's not a knock on the panelists specifically, I think it's pretty common in the field. But it's confusing to listen to, because the implications for how we should prepare are wildly different depending on which world you think we're headed into.

r001.rationale: The candidate questions how near-term AGI could coexist with AI creating more jobs than it displaces, but it does not specify AGI by 2030 or job creation over the following ten years.

astra-6.text: What confused me was that they seemed to be imagining something that could do essentially any cognitive task a human could do, while also predicting that humans would move into new jobs. And I didn’t understand what would prevent the AI from doing those new jobs too. If we’re talking about a technology that automates a particular set of tasks, then sure, people can shift into other work. But if we’re talking about AGI, that argument needs another step: what is it about those new jobs that would give humans an advantage?

r001.rationale: The response questions how broadly capable AI could leave humans new jobs to do, but it does not state the 2030 prediction or that AI would create more jobs than it destroys over the following ten years.

sol-6.1.text: What confused me was that they seemed to be predicting both that we’d have AGI—AI that could do essentially all the cognitive work humans can do—and that there would still be lots of new jobs for humans. And I didn’t understand how those two predictions fit together. If the AI can also do the new jobs, then creating new kinds of work doesn’t necessarily create demand for human workers. So I wanted to understand what they thought humans would be doing, and why AI wouldn’t be able to do that too.

r001.rationale: The response questions how human jobs could persist if AI can do essentially all cognitive work, but it does not state the 2030 timeframe or the prediction that AI will create more jobs than it destroys over the following ten years.
